title: Trump Signed Executive Order 13780, Revising Travel and Refugee Restrictions
description_short: Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017; it temporarily restricted entry for nationals of six countries and paused refugee admissions.
description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780 on March 6, 2017; it took effect March 16. The order suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to stated limits, exceptions and waivers. It separately suspended refugee travel and decisions on refugee-status applications for 120 days and set a 50,000-person ceiling for fiscal-year 2017 admissions. In the Hawaii case, the Ninth Circuit affirmed some injunction provisions and vacated others.
description_long:
President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13780, “Protecting the Nation From Foreign Terrorist Entry Into the United States,” on March 6, 2017. It revoked Executive Order 13769 when it took effect at 12:01 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time on March 16. Section 2 suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen. Section 3 limited that restriction to people outside the United States who lacked a valid visa at 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on January 27 and still lacked one on the order’s effective date. The order listed exceptions, including lawful permanent residents, certain dual nationals, people granted asylum and refugees already admitted, and allowed case-by-case waivers.

Section 6 separately suspended refugee travel and decisions on refugee-status applications under the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program for 120 days, subject to exceptions and waivers, and limited fiscal-year 2017 admissions to 50,000. In the Hawaii case, the Ninth Circuit affirmed parts of a preliminary injunction blocking the entry suspension, refugee-program pause and admissions cap, vacated other parts concerning internal reviews and the President, and remanded. This appellate disposition describes the Hawaii case; it does not combine that case with the separate Maryland litigation.

supported_facts.quote: We affirm in part and vacate in part the district court’s preliminary injunction order. As to the remaining Defendants, we affirm the injunction as to Section 2(c), suspending entry of nationals from the six designated countries for 90 days; Section 6(a), suspending USRAP for 120 days; and Section 6(b), capping the entry of refugees to 50,000 in the fiscal year 2017.

supported_facts.quote: We vacate the portions of the injunction that prevent the Government from conducting internal reviews, as otherwise directed in Sections 2 and 6, and the injunction to the extent that it runs against the President. We remand the case to the district court with instructions to re-issue a preliminary injunction consistent with this opinion.

The revised order suspended entry for 90 days by nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen, subject to stated exceptions, and set a separate 120-day pause on refugee admissions. Iraq was no longer among the six countries. The order stated an effective time of March 16, 2017. Before that date, a federal district court in Hawaii temporarily blocked key provisions; a Maryland district court also enjoined parts of the order, and the government appealed. frozen_original.synopsis: After federal courts blocked the original Muslim ban, Trump signed a revised version on March 6, 2017, Executive Order 13780, which removed Iraq from the list and added exemptions for green card holders and existing visa holders. Courts again blocked the order, with federal judges in Hawaii and Maryland issuing nationwide injunctions before it could take effect. The Fourth and Ninth Circuit Courts of Appeals upheld the injunctions, ruling the order likely violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The administration framed the continued legal battles as judicial overreach. Critics saw the second version as merely cosmetic changes to an unconstitutional religious targeting policy.

rationale: One focused retrieval resolved the description gap for the order and the Hawaii appellate disposition through the Federal Register text and Ninth Circuit opinion. The original AP URL is a 2020 election fact-check, so it is preserved only in research history. The proposal corrects the staged chronology by keeping the Ninth Circuit’s Hawaii disposition separate from Maryland litigation, omitting unsupported Maryland and Fourth Circuit details, and removing the assertion that the Ninth Circuit held EO 13780 likely violated the Establishment Clause; the opinion says it need not consider constitutional claims and affirms injunction provisions on statutory grounds. The prior held204 terminal remains HOLD and unreviewed; this row is only a new editorial proposal, not release approval.
